decisions.quote: Experimental Economics Replication Project Replication of On the Selection of Arbitrators by de Clippel, G./Eliaz, K./Knight, B. (2014) in: The American Economic Review, 104(11), 3434–3458. Replication Authors: Teck Hua Ho, Hang Wu From the perspective of implementation theory, de Clippel et al. compare the performance of two different mechanisms for the selection of arbitrators. They compare the veto-rank mechanism (vr) and shortlisting mechanism ( sl), and find that the latter performs better in terms of efficiency (average aggregate payoff). The main focus of the paper is on the performance of vr vs. sl for two different preference profiles, Pf2 and Pf4. We randomly picked one of the two preference profiles for the replication and ended up with Pf2. Hypothesis to bet on: Efficiency (average aggregate payoff) is higher with the social choice mechanism Shortlisting (sl) than with the Veto-Rank (vr) mechanism for preference profile Pf2.
decisions.location: Primary Project Replication Report (de Clippel et al., 2014), Introduction and Hypothesis to bet on (line 1302); see also Ref. 38 (lines 295-296) and Table S1 (line 1260)
decisions.reason: Both the main manuscript (Ref. 38, Table S1, Table S2) and the individual primary project replication report explicitly identify de Clippel, Eliaz, and Knight (2014), 'On the Selection of Arbitrators', American Economic Review 104(11), 3434-3458, as one of the 18 replicated experimental studies. Shipped and blind target 5 agree on this tested original identity; the spliced quote in the prior blind coding is replaced here with a contiguous literal quote from the primary replication report.

decisions.quote: Replication Results In the replication experiment, the average per round aggregate payoff of 1.705 in the sl treatment is 0.167 higher than in the vr treatment. The difference is statistically significant with p < 0.001 (mean-comparison t-test, t = 7.714). Table 1 summarizes the average per-round aggregate payoffs under the two social choice mechanisms as well as the payoff differences for both the original and the replication study. For Pf2 the outperformance of sl over vr in terms of efficiency is more pronounced in the replication study than the original study. As a measure of effect size we use the difference in average per-round aggregate payoffs between the two treatments. Accordingly, the relative effect size of the replication experiment is 321.12% (0.167/0.052). 2/3 Experimental Economics Replication Project Unplanned Protocol Deviations Discussion The replication experiments were conducted exactly in the way as described above without any deviations from the protocol. Given the criteria and procedure outlined above, the hypothesis of interest has been replicated at a significance level of α < 5%. The relative effect size equals 321.12% and the p-value of the hypothesis test < 0.001.
decisions.location: Primary Project Replication Report (de Clippel et al., 2014), Replication Results and Discussion (line 1302); see also Table S1 (line 1260)
decisions.reason: The individual primary replication report for de Clippel et al. (2014) states an explicit overall verdict that the hypothesis of interest (higher efficiency with Shortlisting than Veto-Rank for preference profile Pf2) was replicated at alpha < 5% (difference = 0.167, p < 0.001, relative effect size = 321.12%), matching 'Replicated = Yes' in Table S1. Both shipped and blind correctly code the outcome as 'successful'.

decisions.quote: The original sample size is 158 participants (70 in the vr treatment and 88 in the sl treatment). To achieve 90% power the required sample size is 153 participants. Sample The sample for replication consists of 156 students (78 participants per treatment, matched in pairs) at the National University of Singapore (NUS). As in the original article, we recruit only undergraduate students from NUS. We use the material of the original experiment (programmed on the web) along with the original instructions, available at the journal’s webpage.
decisions.location: Primary Project Replication Report (de Clippel et al., 2014), Power Analysis, Sample, and Materials (line 1302)
decisions.reason: The study collected new experimental data from a fresh sample of 156 undergraduate students at the National University of Singapore to re-test the published finding of de Clippel, Eliaz, and Knight (2014) (originally conducted at NYU with N = 158), which is a 'replication' under the codebook.

corrected_value.title: Gift Exchange versus Monetary Exchange: Theory and Evidence

decisions.quote:
1. Replications
We replicate 18 experimental studies published between 2011 and 2014 in the high-
impact general interest journals the American Economic Review (AER) and the Quarterly
Journal of Economics (QJE). (33–50) The deadline for inclusion in the study was that the
paper should be published or posted as accepted/in press at the website of the journal at
August 1, 2014.
decisions.location: Supplementary Materials, Section 1. Replications (lines 557-562); see also Ref. 39 (lines 297-298), Table S2 (lines 1162-1165), and Table S1 (line 1261)
decisions.reason: Section 1 of the Supplementary Materials states that the paper replicates the 18 experimental studies cited in References 33-50, where Reference 39 (lines 297-298) is J. Duffy and D. Puzzello, 'Gift exchange versus monetary exchange: Theory and evidence', Am. Econ. Rev. 104, 1735 (2014), and Tables S1 and S2 list Duffy and Puzzello (AER 2014) (Ref. 39) and its tested hypothesis (efficiency comparison between M6 and NM6 treatments). Shipped and blind target 6 agree on this tested original identity, and the spliced quote in the prior blind coding is replaced with a contiguous literal quote.

decisions.quote:
In this article, we provide insights about how well laboratory experiments in economics
replicate. Our sample consists of all 18 between-subject laboratory experimental papers
published in the American Economic Review and the Quarterly Journal of Economics in 2011-
2014. The most important statistically significant finding, as emphasized by the authors of each
paper, was chosen for replication (see the Supplementary Materials, Section 1 and Tables S1 and
S2, for details). We use replication sample sizes with at least 90% power [M=0.92,
median(Mdn)=0.91] to detect the original effect size at the 5% significance level.
